# The AI Hype Cycle Has Caught Up With the Bots

For all the money pouring into generative AI, the technology's real-world performance keeps running into a stubbornly unglamorous wall of mediocre results.

## The Numbers Don't Match the Narrative

A widely circulated Reddit thread on r/ArtificialInteligence claims that AI performs worse than a human 96.25% of the time — a stat that, even if rhetorically generous, captures a sentiment increasingly echoed by practitioners. More rigorously, a peer-reviewed study published in ScienceDirect found that large language models applied to scientific conference summarization showed "persistent deficiencies in speaker coverage, affiliation attribution, and reference citation," despite being able to extract high-level themes and generate readable summaries. In other words, the polish hides the plumbing problems.

## The Trough of Disillusionment Is Real

According to RSM US's 2024 analysis, reality is setting in for AI after many months of hype, and skepticism has grown — fittingly, the technology has slid into what Gartner calls the "trough of disillusionment." Blue Prism's explainer on AI hype versus reality confirms the slide: generative AI projects are failing to deliver value, often because organizations let "a solution looking for a problem" dictate adoption, and because of "poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs and failing to define the business return on investment linkage."

## The Co-Pilot Framing Stuck

Industry voices are landing somewhere between booster and skeptic. Sesh Iyer at BCG X, writing on LinkedIn, framed AI as "a brilliant co-pilot" that can "see patterns we miss, process faster than we ever could, and keep us from getting lost in the fog of" complexity. Yet cloud-computing commentator David Linthicum pushed back in his own LinkedIn post, arguing that "the current AI hype narrative is significantly outpacing reality, setting the stage for a potential reckoning" — particularly around AI coding tools that promise speed but rarely guarantee quality.

## What This Means

The gap between what AI is sold as and what AI actually does is now large enough to demand answers from vendors and patience from buyers. The companies most likely to benefit in the short term are the ones treating AI as a narrowly applied tool rather than a general-purpose replacement for human judgment. As the Dell Technologies podcast "AI: Hype vs. Reality" frames it, the next phase of the cycle depends less on model capability and more on whether organizations can define problems worth solving in the first place.
